description: We are building SPHEREx Change Lens, an evidence-first web tool that compares repeated NASA SPHEREx observations, aligns images, identifies possible changes, and explains the evidence behind each candidate. Our focus is scientific reliability: real data, quality checks, artifact rejection, transparent provenance, and a clear distinction between a candidate requiring follow-up and a confirmed discovery.
summary:
**SPHEREx Change Lens** is an interactive astronomical exploration platform developed by **Team Cosmic Anomaly** for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.

The universe is constantly changing, but identifying stellar motion and brightness variations across massive astronomical datasets can be challenging. NASA's SPHEREx mission provides an opportunity to explore the infrared sky across multiple observations.

Our solution makes this data more accessible by organizing SPHEREx observations into time-ordered sequences. Users can select a sky position, explore aligned images, compare observations across time, and investigate potential changes through a scientific processing pipeline. The system emphasizes data provenance, observation quality, and responsible scientific interpretation by distinguishing potential candidates from confirmed discoveries.

By combining astronomical data processing with an intuitive visual interface, SPHEREx Change Lens aims to bridge the gap between complex scientific datasets and accessible exploration, helping researchers, students, and space enthusiasts investigate how our universe changes over time.
details:
SPHEREx Change Lens

Team Cosmic Anomaly — NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026

Overview

NASA's SPHEREx mission observes the sky in infrared wavelengths, collecting data that can help us study stars, galaxies, and other astronomical objects. With observations taken at different times, there is also an opportunity to investigate how objects move or change.

The problem is that working with this data isn't straightforward. SPHEREx observations come in scientific FITS files containing image data, coordinate information, uncertainty measurements, and calibration details. Comparing observations requires more than simply placing two images side by side.

We built SPHEREx Change Lens to make this process easier.

It's a web application where users can explore real SPHEREx observations, move through observation timelines, inspect potential motion, and review the scientific evidence behind comparisons.

How Our Project Works

We integrated 40 real SPHEREx FITS observations covering five astronomical targets: Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae, and R Draconis.

Each target has eight observations available in our current dataset.

Users can select a target and navigate its observations through a chronological timeline. The application displays aligned image previews, making it easier to inspect the same region of the sky across different observation dates.

We also developed a Python backend that handles astronomical data processing. It includes FITS validation, coordinate transformations, image alignment, source detection, photometry, and motion screening.

The investigation workspace brings together the observations, available motion-screening results, and scientific evidence so users can examine potential changes without having to work directly with the raw files.

Scientific Processing

One of the biggest parts of this project was figuring out how to compare real SPHEREx observations correctly.

Two images of the same target aren't necessarily suitable for direct comparison. SPHEREx observes different infrared wavelengths, and images can also differ in calibration, background brightness, and resolution.

To handle this, we added calibration provenance checks, wavelength compatibility analysis, zodiacal-light subtraction, background preparation, PSF assessment, and uncertainty propagation.

We also built validation checks into the difference-imaging pipeline. If the required scientific information is missing or two observations are incompatible, the system rejects the comparison instead of generating a potentially misleading result.

For example, we investigated two observations of Barnard's Star from September 30 and October 1, 2025. Our initial checks suggested they might be compatible, but further analysis using official calibration data showed that their wavelength ranges did not overlap.

That meant they couldn't be used for a reliable temporal difference image. Our pipeline preserved that rejection.

We haven't completed scientifically validated difference imaging on a real observation pair yet, but the processing and validation components are in place for further work.

Technologies Used

We used TypeScript, Vite, HTML, and CSS for the frontend, with Python, FastAPI, and Uvicorn for the backend.

For the scientific processing, we used Astropy, NumPy, SciPy, Photutils, and Reproject. These libraries handle FITS files, astronomical coordinates, image alignment, source measurements, and numerical calculations.

Our observation data and calibration resources come from NASA/IPAC's Infrared Science Archive (IRSA). We also used IRSA DataLink and publicly available archive storage to retrieve and verify calibration products.

Git and GitHub were used to manage development across our team.

What Makes It Different

We wanted to build something more useful than a gallery of astronomical images.

SPHEREx Change Lens organizes observations by target and time, connects them to scientific processing, and gives users a way to investigate the results in one place.

The application also shows when a comparison cannot be trusted. That's an important part of working with astronomical data because an apparent change in an image doesn't always mean something physically changed in space.

Instead of hiding those limitations, we include them in the investigation process.

Challenges

Working with real SPHEREx data was probably our biggest challenge.

We had to deal with FITS structures, coordinate alignment, different wavelength coverage, calibration dependencies, and uncertainty handling. Getting the observations to display was only one part of the work; determining whether they could be compared was considerably harder.

We successfully integrated and structurally validated all 40 FITS observations in our dataset. We also retrieved official calibration products, verified selected image cutouts against their original observations, and expanded our scientific processing pipeline.

Some scientific work remains, particularly finding compatible observation pairs and completing the validation required for reliable difference imaging.

Impact and Future Work

We built SPHEREx Change Lens for people who want to explore astronomical observations without needing to manually process FITS files or set up a complete scientific analysis environment.

Students and astronomy enthusiasts can use the interface to explore real infrared observations, while the underlying processing components provide a starting point for more detailed investigation.

Our next goal is to identify compatible observations, complete the remaining scientific validation, and display reliable difference images and brightness-change measurements directly in the investigation workspace.

Conclusion

SPHEREx Change Lens brings real NASA infrared observations, chronological image exploration, motion screening, and scientific analysis into one web application.

With this project, our team wanted to make it easier to explore what SPHEREx observes over time, while being careful about what the data can actually tell us.

SPHEREx Change Lens — See how the sky changes.
